models.section: Model of Decision making for Insurance companies
models.summary: An underwriting rule built on information diffusion. One observation of loss is spread over control points by a normal kernel whose width depends on the sample size: a tabulated multiple of the sample range for samples of five to ten, and 2.6851 times the range divided by n minus one from eleven upward. Normalizing the diffused information gives the probability that the loss exceeds a level, the risk index. Premium income in a year is the sum over contracts of the premium rate times the home price, expected claims are the sum of loss probability times loss volume, and profit is the difference. A subsidy returns a coefficient times the claims, so the insurer bears only one minus that coefficient of them. Over n consecutive years every cash flow is discounted to the base year at rate r, and the region is underwritten exactly when the discounted profit is positive. On the demand side a consumer buys only when utility with insurance beats utility without it, so at equilibrium the insurer does not choose the rate freely. With the subsidy computed to be negligible, a zero-profit curve in the plane of disasters per year and premium rate separates the two decisions. Applied to Sichuan over 1999 to 2020 and Slovakia over 2004 to 2020, a grey GM(1,1) forecast puts discounted premiums above discounted claims in every month of the coming year, so both regions are underwritten. The grey test is tight for Sichuan and loose for Slovakia.
models.computational_cost: A grey forecast on 22 and 17 annual observations, plus a zero-profit curve
models.purpose: Decide whether an insurer should underwrite a region and at what rate.
objectives: Underwrite a region exactly when the discounted multi-period profit is positive.

details: The diffusion treats the sample as one batch.
A region is one unit with one risk index.
At market equilibrium the premium rate is set by the owner's utility, not by the insurer.

parameter_estimation.method: The diffusion coefficients are taken from the information diffusion literature. The discount rate is set at 8 percent. The subsidy coefficient is computed from the data and found to be negligible, so it is dropped.

algorithm.description: Diffuse the loss sample, price the book, discount the profit, and forecast.
steps: Choose the diffusion coefficient from the sample size
Normalize the diffused information into a risk index
Compute premiums, claims, and the discounted profit
Forecast the next year with a grey GM(1,1) model and test it
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Not stated. The grey model is judged by precision, variance ratio, and small-probability error.

details: Both regions fall on the underwriting side of the curve.

constraints: The insurer underwrites only when the discounted profit is positive.
The premium rate is constrained by the owner's utility at equilibrium.
strengths: The decision is one sign on a discounted sum, so it is easy to audit.
The same curve serves any region once its disaster count is known.
limitations: The subsidy is computed and then discarded.
The grey forecast for Slovakia has a variance ratio of 0.78, far above the others.

assumptions: The discount rate will not fluctuate significantly.
Every policy is fair and full.

models.section: Model of Site Selection for property developers
models.summary: A siting model grown out of the underwriting one. A developer's decision changes the total property in the region, and the insurer's long-term profit rises with that wealth. A resilience coefficient is the probability that a building shrugs off the disaster, so the adjusted loss is one minus that coefficient times the unadjusted loss, and the insurer's profit rises as resilience rises. The adjusted profit discounts the premium on the new wealth and the surviving loss. For choosing the site, five criteria are named and then folded to four: the extra sustainability cost is written as a coefficient times the traditional construction cost and added to it, and the externality is absorbed into regional demand. The four that remain are regional property price and regional demand, both benefits, and regional risk and total cost, both costs. Scores are normalized to the unit interval, weighted, and ranked by TOPSIS closeness, the distance to the worst solution over the sum of the two distances. The site with the highest index is preferred. No numerical site is computed.
models.computational_cost: A weighted TOPSIS ranking over the candidate regions

models.section: Model for the Conservation of Buildings
models.summary: A conservation choice for a building the insurer will not cover. Value is judged on four dimensions, cultural, historical, economic, and social, weighted by experts at 0.21, 0.36, 0.15, and 0.28, and graded on five degrees from unimportant to extremely important. The grades are spaced evenly in money, at 20, 50, 80, 110, and 140 in units of ten thousand dollars. The building's value is the fuzzy evaluation vector times this grade vector. Loss over the next ten years is discounted at rate r, and the loss rate depends on the option chosen. Four options are costed: in-situ maintenance, in-situ restoration, relocation, and doing nothing. Each cost is the discounted sum of the work plus the discounted loss at that option's loss rate, except relocation, whose loss rate is taken to be about zero so its cost is only the rebuilding. The loss rates are ordered: none is worst, then maintenance, then restoration, and relocation near zero. The chosen option is the cheapest. For the ancient residences of Huizhou the evaluation vector is (0.01, 0.10, 0.19, 0.43, 0.27), the value is 1.055 million dollars, graded very important, and the loss rates are 27.60, 13.33, and 39.88 percent. The four costs come out near 270, 295, 300, and 390 thousand dollars, so in-situ maintenance wins.
